More than half a year after the first excerpt, Er Mu and Fanyu Meng resume their translation of Trevor Cox’s book, this time under a freer Chinese title that means “a history of how human speech evolved.” The editors admit the translation is not original work and the style is less “popular science” than usual, but think it well worth reading for anyone interested in acoustics.

The chapter opens with the 19th-century fight over language. In 1861 the philologist Max Müller declared language the barrier no animal could cross, and Darwin answered with The Descent of Man. Because sound vanishes and neither brains nor vocal organs fossilize, theories of how language arose still provoke fierce disputes; as the science writer Philip Ball put it, the heat of such debates seems inversely proportional to the evidence. Hearing is less contested, helped by fossil ears.

When our four-legged ancestors such as Acanthostega left the water some 350 million years ago, their ears were built for underwater sound. Yet lungfish, close relatives of the early tetrapods, can sense airborne sound: in Christian Christensen’s experiments at Aarhus University, a lightly anesthetized lungfish responded below 200 Hz to sound above 85 dB, through vibration of its whole head. That crude ability gave evolution a starting point. The chapter ends with the mammalian ear: resonance in the ear canal and concha, amplification in the middle ear, and conversion to nerve signals in the cochlea.

Translated into Chinese by Er Mu and reviewed by Fanyu Meng, from Trevor Cox’s Now You’re Talking: Human Conversation from the Neanderthals to Artificial Intelligence (2018). About the book.
